Interviewer: How does your restaurant manager usually lead the team?

Interviewee: Our manager is a really nice person, honestly. He’s always punctual. He arrives at half past ten on the dot and is never late. His clothes are always neat, his leather shoes are polished to a shine and his shirts are always ironed. Among ourselves we say he’s the best-turned-out person in the whole F&B department. His meetings are very well organised too. For the Monday meeting every week he prepares slides and goes through revenue, table turnover and guest review scores page by page. The charts look great and he explains everything very clearly. Last month people from group headquarters came to inspect, and he took them all the way from the private dining rooms to the kitchen and presented everything really smoothly. When the head-office leaders got back, they even praised him by name in an email. Everyone says he’s especially good at giving reports. That’s universally acknowledged. Managers from the other restaurants come to him for his templates, and he once gave a special session in the department group chat on how to turn data into a story. As for what happens on the floor, he usually leaves that to Sister Wang. Sister Wang has worked here for over ten years and knows everything: guest complaints, slow dishes, scheduling and shift swaps. Whenever we have a problem we go to Sister Wang first, and only if she can’t handle it do we go and knock on the manager’s office door. When I first started I couldn’t hold a tray steady, and it was Sister Wang who stayed behind after her shift to teach me. She taught me for almost an hour, and the next day she even brought me an old tray to practise with at home. The manager doesn’t really have much to do with us. When he sees us he nods, and he knows a few of our names. The manager really is a nice person, and we don’t have any conflicts with him. He’s just quite busy, and his office door is usually closed. Sometimes when we’ve finished closing up, his light is still on. He’s probably preparing next week’s report.

Interviewer: A while ago there was a news report about some hotels wiping cups with towels. How are cups usually cleaned here?

Interviewee: We do everything to standard. The cups are taken to the workroom and put into the special disinfection cabinet. Once they’re disinfected they get a plastic seal put over them, and then they go back to the rooms. It was all taught in training, and we were tested on it too. After that news report came out, the hotel even held a special meeting and added two more disinfection cabinets on every floor. Now there are four per floor. One cycle takes forty minutes, and there’s basically no waiting. The disinfection log has to be signed every day as well, and the supervisor collects it before she goes off duty. Each of us has to do sixteen rooms a day, with four cups per room, and at twelve noon the supervisor checks on our progress. There really is a lot of work. Sometimes we don’t even have time for lunch. We’ve raised it with the manager several times, asking whether it could be brought down to fourteen rooms. The manager said he’s considering it, and we still haven’t heard anything. I’m not happy about that, and you can put it in. But when it comes to the cups, nobody dares cut corners. When the supervisor inspects a room, she picks up the cups and holds them up to the light. If there’s the slightest water mark, it has to be redone. Last month a new colleague lost points because of that. She didn’t say anything about it afterwards, and the next day she came in half an hour early to practise. The other floors are the same. It’s standard across the whole hotel. If you’d like to see, I can take you to the workroom in a bit to look at the disinfection cabinets. They’re right by the lifts, and the daily disinfection log is posted by the door. We can also talk about the new bedding we changed to this year while we’re at it. The guest feedback has been really good. You can write about that too. Our manager chose the bedding himself. He cares a lot about it.

Interviewer: Working banquets, have you ever come across guests who were particularly difficult to deal with?

Interviewee: I wouldn’t say difficult. It’s all been within manageable limits. Last month there was a wedding banquet, and at the table next to the head table there was a male guest who’d had quite a lot to drink. He had a really loud voice and kept calling me over to pour wine. He also got me to listen to stories about when he was a young soldier. He went on for almost ten minutes, saying back then he could drink half a kilo of liquor in one sitting. I told him I had other tables to look after and I’d come back and listen later, and he laughed, waved me off, and said, this young lady really knows how to talk. Afterwards I mentioned it to the team leader, and she sent a male colleague over to keep an eye on that table and help keep the pouring under control, so he wouldn’t drink too much and get into trouble. When it finished, his family helped him into the car, and his daughter even came back specially to thank us. She said her dad isn’t usually like that, he was just too happy that day. Guests like that are quite common at weddings, and we practised how to deal with them in training, so I don’t think there was anything difficult about it. Much harder to deal with are the guests who pick at the food: they complain a dish is cold and want it reheated, then once it’s reheated they complain it’s overdone. That wedding banquet actually went really well. They’d booked the Golden Goblet set menu, eighteen courses in all. The lobster and the leopard coral grouper were both prepared on the spot, and the bride’s father even went to the kitchen specially to have his photo taken with the head chef. The banquet department is fully booked again next month with six events, and the manager praised our whole team at the meeting. Recently we’ve been practising a new way of serving dishes. I can do it in three and a half minutes now, which puts me second in the team, and the team leader says I should aim for first at next month’s competition.

Interviewer: I hear your former front-office manager left this year. What was the reason?

Interviewee: Regarding this matter, the hotel has an official position: the employment relationship was terminated by amicable mutual agreement on the basis of personal career planning. That’s what the email said too, and all staff received it. In the month before she left, Finance came to audit the accounts several times, mainly the signatures on some discount slips and complimentary-room slips. What exactly they were checking, we on the cashier side don’t really know. We’re only responsible for submitting the slips according to procedure. The signature box isn’t our concern. During that period her office door was always closed. Twice people from Finance went in and stayed the whole afternoon. Some of the slips were... were instructions passed down from above, and we didn’t... (pauses) Anyway, we on the front line aren’t involved in any of that. Leaving was her personal decision. She didn’t have a meal with everyone. Her husband came by car to collect her things. She was a really nice person. Whenever a guest complained, she’d come out and stand between us and them, and at New Year she’d give each of us a red envelope, out of her own pocket. Oh, by the way, the new manager started last month, and our front-office cashier system has been upgraded too. Now guests can pay by scanning a code, invoices are much quicker, and the queues at peak check-out time are half as long. It used to be that at twelve noon the queue in the lobby would stretch right to the door. Would you like to have a look? I can give you a demonstration. From swiping the key card to printing the invoice, it only takes a minute. The system was procured centrally by the group, and every hotel uses it now.

Interviewer: Is there anything at work that’s made a particularly strong impression on you?

Interviewee: Last month a guest phoned after checking out to say a gold bracelet had gone missing from the bedside table, and I was the one who’d cleaned that room. Security called me into their office and questioned me for almost an hour: what time I went into the room, what time I came out, whether anyone else had come in while I was there. Then, right in front of me, they went through my cleaning trolley and my locker. They even opened my lunch box and looked inside. The office door was open, and every so often a colleague walked past in the corridor, glanced in, and walked on. I kept saying I’d cooperate, that it was only right, the hotel has rules, anyone would have to be checked. The next day the guest found it herself, in the inner pocket of her make-up bag. The lobby manager phoned to tell me it had been a misunderstanding and not to take it to heart. The guest never phoned again after that. I said it’s fine, it’s all over now. For about two weeks after that, I didn’t go to the staff canteen at lunchtime. I just sat in the workroom, and I barely touched the food I’d brought. I also went to bed very late every night when I got home. I lost two kilos in those two weeks. Now when I clean a room, I prop my phone up on the trolley and record from the moment I walk in until I walk out. And I don’t leave the door half open any more. I push it all the way open and wedge it with a doorstop. My team leader asked me once why I do that. I said I’ve just got used to it, and this way everyone can feel easy. Around that time my mum phoned and asked how work was going. I said it’s fine, just a bit tiring, then said I had to go and clean a room, and hung up. Actually, I’d already finished my shift that day.

Interviewer: How does your manager usually get on with everyone?

Interviewee: The biggest thing about our manager is that he loves telling cold jokes, the really corny kind. He tells one at the morning briefing every single day, and when he’s finished he’s the first to laugh. For example, he says: why can’t eggs tell jokes? Because they’d crack up. Not one person in the room laughs. He’s the only one there enjoying himself. I’ve told him several times: boss, that joke really isn’t funny, could you stop telling them, you’re wasting everyone’s time. He says no, it’s his tradition. But in the notes app on my phone I’ve got a folder just for the jokes he’s told. I’ve recorded more than 120 so far, with the date written after each one. Some of them I’ve even marked with a star. Those are the ones I think are especially cold, so cold I wanted to walk out on the spot. Last time he went to head office for two weeks’ training, nobody told jokes at the morning briefing. On the third day I told one myself, the egg one, and even laughed first the way he does. My colleagues teased me about it all morning. The day he came back, he told a new one right at the start of the briefing, and I wrote it down in my notes there and then. At the department dinner at the end of the year, I printed all these jokes out, bound them into a little booklet and gave it to him. On the cover I wrote: The Complete Cold Jokes, Volume One. When he got it he stood there stunned for quite a while. Since then that booklet has stayed on his desk. Once I saw him flipping through it, and when he got to a certain page he laughed out loud by himself. So, our manager is great in every way, it’s just that his jokes are too cold. They’re so cold we don’t need the air conditioning in summer. I really can’t stand him.

Interviewer: This year the hotel brought in a new rule that frontline staff can approve compensation of up to 500 yuan themselves. How has that worked out in the concierge team?

Interviewee: It’s all right, I guess. It’s just a small change to the procedure, and it doesn’t make much difference to us in the concierge team. We very rarely have to actually pay out compensation. Most of the time we’re booking cars, storing luggage, recommending restaurants and buying show tickets for guests. Things that need compensation come up maybe once or twice a month, and the amounts are mostly very small, like an umbrella wrecked by the wind or a cake box squashed in storage, a few dozen yuan at most. Before, if a guest’s luggage got damaged, we had to phone the duty manager first. Now we can deal with it ourselves first and just fill in a form afterwards. I’ve only used it once so far. Last month a guest’s suitcase handle got caught on our luggage trolley and snapped, and I put in 120 yuan for the repair. I filled in the form the same day and my supervisor signed it without saying anything. The guest was very polite about it. He said it was an old suitcase anyway and there was no need to pay. I still put it through according to the rules and wrote the reason clearly on the form, so there wouldn’t be any confusion later. The front desk uses it more. They get more complaints than we do: room problems, noise, breakfast, all sorts. They say it really has made things a lot easier. They used to phone the duty manager seven or eight times a night, and now it’s less than half that. I heard the rule was brought in by the group across the board, the same at every hotel, and Finance puts together a summary once a month to see how much each department has used. We don’t really know how they came up with the figure of 500. Anyway, for me, it just means fewer phone calls, I suppose. Nothing much else has changed.

Interviewer: Your floor got a new team leader this year. How is everyone getting on with her?

Interviewee: The new team leader is a young woman born after 1995, poached from another hotel. I heard she was known over there for being strict. She’s not much older than my daughter. Interviewer: How much of the banquet service charge do you frontline staff get?

Interviewee: The service charge is distributed centrally according to hotel regulations. The formula is set out clearly in the staff handbook. It’s calculated using a length-of-service coefficient and a grade coefficient, and the breakdown is posted on the noticeboard once a month. There’s a line on the payslip called service bonus. I check it every month and take a photo of it on my phone to keep. To be honest, I’m not happy with the formula. Someone like me who’s been here three years has a coefficient of 1.0, and a long-serving employee with ten years has 1.8. But at the three weddings every weekend, it’s basically us young ones carrying the drinks, moving the tables and chairs and clearing up. The long-serving staff just stand to one side giving directions, and they get nearly twice as much as we do. Last year I asked once in the group chat whether the number of events worked could be included too. My supervisor said that would have to wait to be discussed at the staff representatives’ meeting, and told me to write a proposal. I wrote it and handed it in. This year’s meeting is next month, and I’m going to raise it again. Seven or eight colleagues have already signed it. My supervisor didn’t say anything against it, and even reminded me to get the numbers right and not make any mistakes. Actually, the benefits here are pretty good overall. Meals and accommodation are included. The dorm rooms are for two people, with air conditioning and a washing machine. It’s much better than the hotel I was at before. There’s also a year-end bonus. Last year it was a month and a half’s pay. It’s just the service charge part that I think is unfair. You can write that as it is, and you can put my name on it too. Next month is the peak wedding season. Every weekend we’ll have three events, and everyone’s bound to start talking about this again. I hope we get a result this year.

Interviewer: You were promoted to supervisor this year. How does it feel?

Interviewee: It’s just a change of title, really. The work’s still the same. This time the decision was made following a comprehensive departmental assessment. There were several candidates, none of us knew the outcome, and the list was posted on Friday afternoon. Ah Fang applied too. She’s actually better suited than me. She makes beds faster than I do, she’s had more letters of praise from guests, and last year she won second prize in the housekeeping skills competition. The two of us joined in the same intake. We used to share a dorm, do night shifts together, and go for malatang together after work. One Spring Festival neither of us went home, and we made dumplings together in the dorm. After the new staff badge was issued, I kept it in my bag for a week before I started wearing it. That evening when I got home, I took it out again, put it on the table and looked at it for a while. I took a photo and sent it to my dad. He replied with a thumbs-up, then phoned and asked me all sorts of questions: how many people I’m in charge of, how much my pay went up, whether I should treat the relatives to a meal. Interviewer: What’s the atmosphere like in your department?

Interviewee: The atmosphere couldn’t be better. Our supervisor often says our department is one big family, we’re all family here. We’re family, after all, so of course nobody keeps score. This Spring Festival I worked twelve days straight. On New Year’s Eve I worked from seven in the morning until eleven at night, running back and forth between the lobby, the lifts and the toilets. We’re family, after all, so of course we should be together at New Year. New Year’s Eve dinner was a box of dumplings handed out by the canteen. I ate it in the store room, then went straight back to mopping. Xiao Li in our team, his grandmother was in hospital, and he wanted to take two days off to go back and see her. The supervisor told him, as family you can’t just walk away from your duties at a time like this, everyone’s holding the fort, if you leave who’s going to cover for you? So in the end Xiao Li didn’t go. We’re family, after all, we have to be understanding with each other. The day his grandmother was discharged, he phoned home from the stairwell, and after the call he stood there for a long time. About overtime pay, someone asked once in the group chat. The supervisor said, among family, talking about money just hurts feelings, it’ll all be considered together at the end of the year. The result of considering it all together at the end of the year was that everyone got a bottle of cooking oil and a thank-you card, and on the card was the word family again. At the end of the year our supervisor was named one of the group’s Outstanding Managers. When he went up on stage to give his speech at the award ceremony, he said what he was proudest of was building a team that’s like a family, that doesn’t make demands and doesn’t count the cost. At that point he even paused to wipe his eyes. All of us in the audience applauded, and I clapped pretty hard. Honestly, a department as warm as ours really is hard to find these days. Interviewer: You were promoted to supervisor this year. How does it feel?

Interviewer: The hotel switched to a new front-desk system this year. How have you found it?

Interviewee: The new system was rolled out across the whole group. At the training, the instructor said it would raise efficiency by thirty percent. At first I didn’t really believe it. I thought it was just the official line, because when has changing systems ever been painless? Two months in, it really is a lot faster. You scan the guest’s ID card and the details fill in automatically, and the deposit can be paid by scanning a code. Guests spend much less time standing at the desk, and we don’t have to keep apologising while we wait for pages to load. Once last month a tour group arrived, more than forty people coming into the lobby at once. Before, they’d have queued for at least half an hour. I used to copy out the reservations by hand every day when I started my shift, in a hardcover notebook I bought myself, because I was afraid of making mistakes. That notebook has been sitting in my drawer untouched for ages now. The system flags duplicate names, overbooking and insufficient deposits automatically, and checks more carefully than I did myself, so we don’t have to go through the notebook at handover any more either. Our night-shift colleagues say the night audit takes almost an hour less than before, so they can hand over and go home earlier, and if there’s a problem they call the support hotline and someone gets back to them within ten minutes. Last week the manager showed us the figures: the average queuing time went down from eight minutes to five. The interface also looks better than the old one: the colours and icons are all very clear. Honestly, I really do think switching systems was the right call this time.
